1.pericope_label: The word against Babylon: Bel is confounded, Merodach broken in pieces, and a nation cometh up out of the north
debates: Whether the prophecy is genuinely Jeremiah own
Whether Bel and Merodach are two gods, one god, or a god and a king
What the standard of the second verse is for
outliers: Calvin says he does not know why some make Merodach an idol, taking the name for a king well known to the Jews, where Henry, Wesley and Clarke make the pair two chief idols and Ellicott makes them two names of one deity
Keil and Delitzsch report critics who deny the prophecy to Jeremiah or treat it as an interpolation, and set out the case for its genuineness
themes: A prophecy defended against its own critics
Ruin foretold of a king who had been kind to the prophet
Beacons rather than banners
A phrase turned back on the nation that once fulfilled it

4.pericope_label: Israel and Judah shall come weeping and ask the way to Zion, for my people hath been lost sheep
debates: Whether the promise is fulfilled in the return under Cyrus or looks further
Whether the word rendered thitherward should be hitherward
How far the fault of the shepherds excuses the flock
outliers: Wesley reads the return literally of the decree of Cyrus, Gill denies that asking the way suits that return at all and refers it to a later conversion, and Clarke reads the verses as a portrait of penitents in any age
Calvin agrees with Ellicott that the text reads hitherward rather than thitherward, both taking it as evidence that the prophecy was written in Judah
themes: Deliverance tied to the ruin of the oppressor
A divided people promised back as one body
A single adverb used as evidence of authorship
Blame laid on the shepherds without acquitting the sheep

8.pericope_label: Remove out of the midst of Babylon: an assembly of great nations from the north, and Chaldea shall be a spoil
debates: How the order to leave squares with the earlier order to settle
Whether from thence is a note of time or of place
Whether the clause about returning in vain belongs to the archer or the arrow
outliers: Ellicott sets this command against the counsel Jeremiah had earlier sent the exiles to build and plant, and resolves the two by saying the earlier advice was right for its time only
Ellicott renders the leading animal a ram where Clarke, Wesley and Calvin keep the he-goat and build on its boldness
themes: A command to flee that presupposes the door already open
An army described as an assembly because it was convened
A city to be taken at one stroke and not besieged twice
Plunderers who admit they have enough

11.pericope_label: Ye destroyers of mine heritage: your mother shall be sore confounded, and every one that goeth by shall hiss
debates: What the charge against Babylon actually is
Whether the second animal of the eleventh verse is a bull or a horse
What the clause about the hindermost of the nations describes
outliers: Ellicott and Calvin agree in reading the second figure as neighing steeds rather than bellowing bulls, Calvin adding that those who keep the bulls must alter the verb to suit them
Wesley traces the judgment to luxury attending wealth, where Gill and Calvin trace it to the exulting of the Chaldeans over a ruined people
themes: A commission to destroy exceeded by the men who held it
A heifer fattened on the floor it was treading
A capital city called the mother of its own people
An empire reduced to the dregs of the nations

14.pericope_label: Put yourselves in array against Babylon: she hath given her hand, and cut off the sower from Babylon
debates: What sin of Babylon is meant when it is said she sinned against the Lord
What the fallen foundations are
Whether the prophecy was fulfilled by Cyrus or reaches further
outliers: Ellicott asks whether the psalmist heard this prophecy or the prophet heard the psalm, since the closing charge is almost word for word a psalm, and judges the first the likelier
Calvin says the cutting off of sower and reaper was not fulfilled by Cyrus, whose assault was only a prelude to later calamities
themes: A prophet commanding armies he will never address
Wrong done to the faithful counted as done to God
A hand stretched out in surrender and in treachery at once
Corn fields inside the walls of a besieged city

17.pericope_label: Israel a scattered sheep driven by lions: I will bring him again to his pasture, and his iniquity shall not be found
debates: Whether the restoration promised is the return from Babylon or something later
Whether the nineteenth verse speaks of the ten tribes or of the whole nation
What the pardon of the twentieth verse remits
outliers: Clarke refers the nineteenth verse wholly to the ten tribes on the ground of the districts named, where Gill takes it of the whole nation and denies that it was fulfilled at the return from Babylon
Clarke and Wesley read the pardon as remission of punishment, where Calvin makes remission of guilt the primary thing and deliverance only its consequence
themes: A sheep devoured twice over by successive empires
One fallen empire offered as security for the fall of another
Chastisement described as medicine rather than sentence
A sick man who asks only that the pain be stopped

21.pericope_label: Go up against Merathaim and Pekod: how is the hammer of the whole earth cut asunder, and Babylon taken unaware
debates: Whether Merathaim and Pekod are place names or descriptions
What the hammer of the whole earth is
Why the fall is put as a question of astonishment
outliers: Gill, Henry and Wesley take both names for real places on the route of Cyrus, Clarke denies that places are meant at all, and Ellicott splits the difference by making the first a coined description and the second a genuine town chosen for its meaning
Calvin dismisses as groundless the identification of the second name with a town of note, and as frigid the alternative that it was a mean and obscure place
themes: Names chosen so that they sentence what they name
Empires described as weapons kept in a divine armoury
A hammer broken by a heavier one
A river drained to open a gate

25.pericope_label: The Lord hath opened his armoury: slay all her bullocks, and declare in Zion the vengeance of his temple
debates: What the armoury of the Lord stands for
Whether the storehouses are granaries and the heaps heaps of corn
Whether the bullocks are the great men or the offspring
outliers: Ellicott renders the storehouses granaries and the heaps heaps of corn, where Calvin calls granary too narrow for a word that covers wine and money and weapons alike, and where his own editor prefers heaps of rubbish
A reading recorded beside Calvin takes the word rendered bullocks for offspring, on the strength of two versions and a parallel passage
themes: A word for treasury translated arsenal by its context
A city that fell with its walls undamaged
Slaughter described as a descent
Deliverance that lays an obligation to speak

29.pericope_label: Call together the archers against Babylon: I am against thee, O thou most proud, and none shall raise him up
debates: Whether the word at the head of the summons means archers, many, or the mighty
Whether the word rendered most proud is a title or a name
What the fire kindled in his cities stands for
outliers: Calvin prefers the mighty to the archers of the received text and dismisses the rendering arrows outright, the noun by itself never bearing that sense
Gill reports a commentator who fixes the proud one on the king killed the night the city fell, and prefers to take it of the whole monarchy
themes: A name for the enemy coined out of his chief vice
Men killed in their own streets rather than in the field
Rescue declared useless rather than unattempted
A first appearance in this book of a title borrowed from an older prophet

33.pericope_label: Israel and Judah oppressed together, but their Redeemer is strong: a sword upon the Chaldeans and upon her wise men
debates: Whether the oppression is described as past or present
Whether the land is to be given rest or set in commotion
What the word rendered liars means
outliers: Ellicott would render the clause that God gives rest to the earth, and reports versions and commentators who instead make the verb mean to trouble; Calvin adopts that second sense outright, and his own editor answers that no instance of the form bears it

Gill, Ellicott and Calvin all abandon the received rendering liars, Gill and Calvin for diviners and Ellicott for prating fools, and Gill rejects the marginal bars because the great men are named both before and after
themes: A present tense that explains why the future judgment is needed
A redeemer defined as the next of kin
Astrologers granted the name of wise men only by courtesy
An art called praiseworthy in itself and ruinous in practice

37.pericope_label: A sword upon her treasures and a drought upon her waters: wild beasts shall dwell there, as when God overthrew Sodom
debates: Whether the thirty-eighth verse threatens a sword or a drought
Which creatures the three names of the thirty-ninth verse denote
How a sentence of perpetual desolation squares with the later history of the city
outliers: Clarke keeps the sword in the thirty-eighth verse, the original word being the same as in the verses before, where Calvin says a single point changes it to drought and reports the versions divided
Calvin declines to contend over the names of the creatures, taking them for birds and beasts of the forest rather than satyrs and fairies, where Ellicott and Clarke press particular identifications
themes: A city defended by a river and entered along its bed
A word altered by one point
Ruin pronounced absolutely and fulfilled by stages
One overthrow set up as a mirror for all others

41.pericope_label: A people cometh from the north with bow and lance: the king of Babylon hath heard the report, and his hands waxed feeble
debates: Who the many kings of the forty-first verse are
Whether the second weapon named is a lance or a shield
How the sudden collapse squares with the length of the siege
outliers: Calvin rejects as untrue the admiring Greek life of Cyrus that Gill draws his military detail from, calling its author no true historian and Cyrus a barbarian who delighted in slaughter
Gill reports a paraphrase rendering the second weapon a shield, which Calvin sets aside for spear or lance
themes: One passage serving two opposite armies
A commander who was chief without being king
Victory won before the battle by report alone
A collapse that took a long siege to arrive at

44.pericope_label: He shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan: hear the counsel of the Lord, and the earth is moved
debates: Why the chapter closes by repeating an earlier oracle
What the lion from the swelling of Jordan is
Why the counsel and purposes of God are named
outliers: Calvin sets aside the reading that makes the phrase the pride of Jordan, preferring a lion driven from its lair by the flooding of the river
Calvin takes the forty-fifth verse for an oath with an elliptical form, where Gill and Clarke treat it simply as a repetition of the earlier passage
themes: An oracle reused against the nation that first fulfilled it
A lion made fiercer by being driven from home
Deliberation ascribed to God only by way of speaking
An objection answered before it is raised
